title: Direct products, direct sums, and element orders
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ The Classification of Finite Abelian Groups
terms: direct product of groups; finite direct sum; coordinatewise operation; order in a direct product; cyclic product criterion.

exposition.text:
The direct product G × H has pairs as elements and coordinatewise operations. Its order is
|G||H| when both factors are finite, and an element (g, h) of finite component orders has order
lcm(ord g, ord h). For finitely many Abelian factors, direct product and direct sum agree.
A product Z × Z is cyclic exactly when gcd(m, n) = 1, and then is isomorphic to Z . For
m n mn
more finite cyclic factors, the orders must be pairwise coprime. Infinite direct products and
direct sums differ: the sum allows only finitely many nonidentity coordinates, whereas the prod-
uct does not impose that restriction.
The support of a sequence is the set of coordinates where it is not the identity. A direct sum
permits only finite support. Thus the countable sum of copies of Z is countable, while their
2
full product is uncountable. Subgroups can also link coordinates: the diagonal {(g, g)} is a
subgroup of G × G isomorphic to G.

question.text:
What is the order of (6, 10, 9) in Z × Z × Z ?
18 25 21
(A) 15 (B) 21 (C) 35 (D) 105 (E) 315

solution.text:
The component orders are 18/6 = 3, 25/5 = 5, and 21/3 = 7. Their least common multiple
is 105.

question.text:
How many elements of Z × Z have order exactly 4?
4 12
(A) 4 (B) 6 (C) 8 (D) 12 (E) 16

solution.text:
The equation 4x = 0 has four solutions in each factor, giving 16 elements whose order di-
vides four. The equation 2x = 0 has two solutions per factor, giving four with order divid-
ing two. Subtract to get 16 − 4 = 12.

Let S = Z and P = Z . Which cardinality statement is correct?
2 2

(A) Both are finite.
(B) Both are countably infinite.
(C) S is countably infinite and P is uncountable.
(D) S is uncountable and P is countably infinite.
(E) Both have exactly two elements.

solution.text:
An element of S is a binary sequence with only finitely many ones, specified by a finite
subset of the natural numbers. There are countably many such subsets. Elements of P are
all binary sequences, an uncountable set by the diagonal argument. Finite direct sums and
products agree, but this infinite distinction is substantial.

question.text:
Which element belongs to the cyclic subgroup generated by (1, 1) in Z × Z ?
2
(A) (0, 1) (B) (1, 0) (C) (2, 0) (D) (3, 0) (E) (4, 1)

solution.text:
The integer multiples of (1, 1) are (k, k mod 2). Only (2, 0) among the choices satisfies this
relation. The generator has infinite order, yet its subgroup is proper because it omits (0, 1).

question.text:
Let D = {(g, g) : g ∈ S } ⊆ S × S . Which statement is true?

(A) D is not closed under multiplication.
(B) D is a subgroup of order six.
(C) D is a cyclic subgroup of order six.
(D) D has order thirty-six.
(E) D is an Abelian subgroup.

stay in D. The map g 7→ (g, g) is an isomorphism from S to D, so D has six elements
